Series::StatAccessor::skewness¶

Back to Series::StatAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::StatAccessor::skewness() const
Series Series::StatAccessor::skewness(std::int64_t dim) const
Series SeriesStatProxy::skewness() const
Series SeriesStatProxy::skewness(std::int64_t dim) const

What It Does¶

skewness() measures standardized third-moment asymmetry. Positive values indicate a longer or heavier right tail, negative values a longer or heavier left tail, and zero a symmetric lane. Zero does not mean low variance.

The statistic is dimensionless: translating a lane or multiplying it by a positive scale does not change its skewness. It is a reduction, so global and axis-wise calls describe different populations rather than transforming the owner.

Parameters And Returns¶

Omit dim to pool every value. Supply a valid, possibly negative dim to return one skewness per surviving lane. The global result currently has shape [1].

Examples¶

Example 1. Symmetric rows have zero third-moment asymmetry.

auto symmetric = pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, {2, 3});
std::cout << symmetric.stat.skewness(1) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0]

Example 2. Repeated low values and one high value create positive skewness.

auto lopsided = pluss::make_series({1, 1, 4, 2, 2, 8}, {2, 3});
std::cout << lopsided.stat().skewness(1) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.70710678, 0.70710678]

Example 3. Pooling both rows creates a different distribution; global skewness is not the average of the row statistics.

std::cout << lopsided.stat.skewness() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[1.2247449]

Pooling the rows changes the population being described, so global skewness is not an average of row skewness. Here it is larger than either row result.

Interpreting The Statistic¶

Skewness is dimensionless because deviations are normalized by standard deviation. Multiplying every value by a positive constant therefore changes spread but not skewness. Treat estimates from very short lanes cautiously; higher moments are sensitive to a few extreme observations.
